passages.title: The hearers' received faith becomes an example during continued suffering
passages.summary: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the assembly of the Thessalonians. They thank God for the readers’ faith, love, and enduring hope. The good news came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit. They received the word in much affliction with joy. They became an example to believers in Macedonia and Achaia. People everywhere tell how they turned from idols to serve the living God. They wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sincere sharing through a faithful personal example. How does receiving the message amid suffering become an example to others?

contextNote.title: The hearers' received faith becomes an example during continued suffering
contextNote.text: Verse 5 says the readers saw what kind of men the writers were. Verse 6 says the readers then became imitators of them and of the Lord. The likeness is specific. They received the word in much affliction. They also received it with joy from the Holy Spirit. Trouble and joy together is the pattern they copied. Verse 7 shows it passing on: they became an example to other believers.

passages.title: Remembered care supports trust while painful separation remains unresolved
passages.summary: Paul recalls that they came to Thessalonica after being mistreated at Philippi. They did not use flattery or seek glory or money. They were gentle, like a nursing mother with her children. They worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. They urged each one as a father does. The readers accepted the message as God’s word and suffered from their own countrymen. Paul speaks sharply of those in Judea who opposed the assemblies there. He wanted to return, but Satan hindered him, and the readers are his joy.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sharing the gospel with sincerity and love. Why does Paul ask the hearers to remember the teachers' own conduct?

contextNote.title: Remembered care supports trust while painful separation remains unresolved
contextNote.text: Verses 3–6 deny wrong motives: deceit, flattery, greed, and a search for glory. Verse 7 gives the opposite picture: a nursing mother. Verse 8 says what that care amounted to. They gave the good news, and they gave their own souls. The reason is affection: the readers had become very dear to them. Verse 9 offers proof the readers can remember: labor night and day.

passages.title: Timothy's report turns fear about separation into comfort and renewed prayer
passages.summary: Paul could not bear the separation and sent Timothy from Athens. Timothy was to strengthen them so that no one would be shaken by afflictions. Paul had warned them that suffering would come. He feared the tempter had tempted them and the work was wasted. Timothy has now returned with good news of their faith and love. Paul says he lives if they stand firm in the Lord. He prays night and day to see them and supply what their faith lacks. He prays that their love will increase.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Thessalonians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects increased love with growing holiness. How does Timothy's report give comfort to the teachers as well as the hearers?

contextNote.title: Timothy's report turns fear about separation into comfort and renewed prayer
contextNote.text: Verse 5 states Paul’s fear: the tempter may have undone the work. He sent Timothy because he could bear it no longer. Verse 6 reports the answer, and it has three parts. Their faith holds, their love holds, and they remember the writers kindly. The third part matters to a man torn away from them (2:17). They long to see him as he longs to see them. Verse 7 says this comforted him in his own distress.

passages.title: Careful conduct and hope for the dead answer different forms of harm and fear
passages.summary: Paul urges them to live so as to please God, more and more. God’s will is their holiness, and they are to abstain from sexual immorality. No one should wrong a brother in this matter. They already love one another and should do so more. They should live quietly, mind their own business, and work with their hands. Paul then writes about those who have fallen asleep. The dead in Christ will rise first, when the Lord descends with a shout. Then the living will be caught up to be with the Lord always.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches gradual growth in holiness and work that supports others. Why does the account of the dead end with shared comfort?

contextNote.title: Careful conduct and hope for the dead answer different forms of harm and fear
contextNote.text: Verse 13 gives the purpose of the passage. Paul does not want them to grieve like those who have no hope. The worry seems to be that the dead will miss the Lord’s coming. Verse 15 answers it: the living will not go ahead of the dead. Verse 16 puts the dead in Christ first. Verse 17 ends with all of them together with the Lord. Verse 18 tells them to use these words to comfort each other.

passages.title: An unknown day calls for alert care rather than a calculated schedule
passages.summary: Paul says they need no letter about times and seasons. The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. They are children of light and should stay awake and sober. They wear faith and love as a breastplate and hope as a helmet. They should respect those who labor among them and lead them. Paul gives short commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. They should not quench the Spirit, and they should test all things. He asks that the letter be read to all the brothers.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

lds.text: How do different needs require different kinds of care?

contextNote.title: An unknown day calls for alert care rather than a calculated schedule
contextNote.text: Verses 12–13 speak of those who lead. Verse 14 then gives a task to the “brothers,” the whole group. It names three kinds of people and three different responses. The disorderly are admonished, the faint-hearted encouraged, and the weak supported. One response covers everyone: patience. Verse 15 adds the limit: no one may repay evil for evil.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: 1 Thessalonians: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Remembered care supports trust while painful separation remains unresolved
steps.text: Verses 3–6 deny wrong motives: deceit, flattery, greed, and a search for glory. Verse 7 gives the opposite picture: a nursing mother. Verse 8 says what that care amounted to. They gave the good news, and they gave their own souls. The reason is affection: the readers had become very dear to them. Verse 9 offers proof the readers can remember: labor night and day.

steps.title: Timothy's report turns fear about separation into comfort and renewed prayer
steps.text: Verse 5 states Paul’s fear: the tempter may have undone the work. He sent Timothy because he could bear it no longer. Verse 6 reports the answer, and it has three parts. Their faith holds, their love holds, and they remember the writers kindly. The third part matters to a man torn away from them (2:17). They long to see him as he longs to see them. Verse 7 says this comforted him in his own distress.

steps.title: Careful conduct and hope for the dead answer different forms of harm and fear
steps.text: Verse 13 gives the purpose of the passage. Paul does not want them to grieve like those who have no hope. The worry seems to be that the dead will miss the Lord’s coming. Verse 15 answers it: the living will not go ahead of the dead. Verse 16 puts the dead in Christ first. Verse 17 ends with all of them together with the Lord. Verse 18 tells them to use these words to comfort each other.

steps.title: An unknown day calls for alert care rather than a calculated schedule
steps.text: Verses 12–13 speak of those who lead. Verse 14 then gives a task to the “brothers,” the whole group. It names three kinds of people and three different responses. The disorderly are admonished, the faint-hearted encouraged, and the weak supported. One response covers everyone: patience. Verse 15 adds the limit: no one may repay evil for evil.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the assembly of the Thessalonians. They thank God for the readers’ faith, love, and enduring hope. The good news came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit. They received the word in much affliction with joy. They became an example to believers in Macedonia and Achaia. People everywhere tell how they turned from idols to serve the living God. They wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul recalls that they came to Thessalonica after being mistreated at Philippi. They did not use flattery or seek glory or money. They were gentle, like a nursing mother with her children. They worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. They urged each one as a father does. The readers accepted the message as God’s word and suffered from their own countrymen. Paul speaks sharply of those in Judea who opposed the assemblies there. He wanted to return, but Satan hindered him, and the readers are his joy.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

chapterMaps.note: Lines join the places 1 Thessalonians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul could not bear the separation and sent Timothy from Athens. Timothy was to strengthen them so that no one would be shaken by afflictions. Paul had warned them that suffering would come. He feared the tempter had tempted them and the work was wasted. Timothy has now returned with good news of their faith and love. Paul says he lives if they stand firm in the Lord. He prays night and day to see them and supply what their faith lacks. He prays that their love will increase.
chapterMaps.limits: Lines join the places 1 Thessalonians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul urges them to live so as to please God, more and more. God’s will is their holiness, and they are to abstain from sexual immorality. No one should wrong a brother in this matter. They already love one another and should do so more. They should live quietly, mind their own business, and work with their hands. Paul then writes about those who have fallen asleep. The dead in Christ will rise first, when the Lord descends with a shout. Then the living will be caught up to be with the Lord always.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the city addressed and the cities Paul names from his past work.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says they need no letter about times and seasons. The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. They are children of light and should stay awake and sober. They wear faith and love as a breastplate and hope as a helmet. They should respect those who labor among them and lead them. Paul gives short commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. They should not quench the Spirit, and they should test all things. He asks that the letter be read to all the brothers.
